title: Syntax, Compile-Time, Runtime, and Logic Errors
learningObjectives: Describe the main idea and its role in reliable program behavior.
Recognize the topic in code or a real-world programming scenario.
Trace the relevant behavior and identify the likely outcome.
Explain a common mistake, risk, or limitation.
Apply the concept and verify the result with a suitable check.

understand.concept: Errors can arise at different stages: syntax or compile-time checks reject code before it can run; runtime errors occur while execution is underway; logic errors let a program run but produce incorrect results. The exact stage names depend on the language and toolchain. Some languages compile, some interpret, and many use mixed pipelines.
understand.whyItMatters: Classifying an error narrows the investigation. Syntax and compile-time errors usually point to source or type rules, runtime errors to execution conditions, and logic errors to assumptions or algorithms.
understand.analogy: A recipe may be written in an invalid format, contain an instruction that cannot be carried out with available equipment, or have a valid instruction that yields the wrong dish. Software errors differ from recipes but the stages help separate causes.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only a simplified comparison; software failures and recovery depend on language, runtime, system boundaries, and context.

explain.narrative: Read the message and identify when the failure occurs. Check syntax and diagnostics first, then trace runtime conditions, then verify the algorithm and expected result. Avoid treating every incorrect output as a runtime crash.

examples.title: Missing delimiter
examples.expectedOutput: A syntax error may be reported before execution.
examples.explanation: A missing language-required delimiter can prevent parsing.

examples.title: Invalid name
examples.expectedOutput: A runtime ReferenceError occurs if totalPrice was never defined.
examples.explanation: The source may parse, but execution references a missing name.

examples.title: Wrong calculation
examples.explanation: The code runs but precedence may not match the intended calculation.

examples.title: Unexpected input
examples.explanation: Input conversion may produce a special value instead of a usable number.

examples.title: Correcting the expectation
examples.explanation: Grouping makes the intended order explicit and fixes the logic.

commonMistakes: Calling every failure a syntax error.
Ignoring the first diagnostic and focusing on later cascading messages.
Assuming a program that runs is correct.
Changing several lines at once without retesting.
Confusing expected output with observed output.

independentTask.title: Independent practice: Syntax, Compile-Time, Runtime, and Logic Errors
independentTask.instructions: Create a small original program or pseudocode scenario applying this topic.
requirements: Implement the topic with clear behavior.
Include at least one normal case and one failure or edge case.

hints: Start by defining expected behavior precisely.
Inspect the earliest relevant failure or boundary.
Make one change at a time and retest.
Keep user-facing messages useful and safe.
Verify both normal and failure paths.
